name: A2RL Drone Championship
ability_definition: The ability to quickly and repeatedly adjust the controls of a machine or a vehicle to exact positions.

task_realism.reasoning: The task is real vehicle control. A physical drone must be steered through exact gate positions using rapid, repeated motor-level adjustments, which is the core of the ability. However, high-speed racing through a fixed gate course is a niche activity. It differs from typical workplace precision control, such as operating cranes, forklifts, surgical or industrial machinery, or inspection drones, where the emphasis is on careful, exact positioning rather than minimizing lap time.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Conditions are unusually realistic for an AI benchmark. The system uses real hardware and real physics, with onboard-only compute and sensing. There is no human intervention, no external localization, and genuine time pressure and failure stakes. On the other hand, the environment is a controlled arena with a known, pre-surveyed course. There are few runs at a single annual event, and there is no variation in payload, weather, or operational context of the kind real work involves.

construct_coverage.reasoning: Coverage is narrow. There is one vehicle type (quadrotor), one task type (gate racing), and one metric (lap time). Lap time mixes perception and planning with control, and it rewards speed rather than directly measuring positional exactness or consistency across repetitions. The benchmark does not cover diverse machines, control interfaces, or fine positioning tasks such as stopping at exact setpoints.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are real onboard sensor streams, and outputs are direct 500 Hz motor commands to real actuators, which is an authentic control format rather than multiple choice or a toy grid. The scoring artifact, a press-reported lap time, is coarse. It is not the kind of precision or tolerance measure used to judge real machine operation, and the course layout is artificial.

transferability_reasoning: A2RL is one of the few benchmarks where an AI directly and rapidly actuates a real vehicle to reach exact positions, so its realism and format are genuinely strong for Control Precision. Transfer is limited because it covers one racing-specific vehicle task and a single lap-time metric that mixes in perception and planning. It also does not directly measure positional accuracy or consistency across the range of machines seen in workplace control.

2025.model_or_system: TU Delft MAVLab autonomous drone (G&CNet direct motor-control policy)
2025.metric: seconds to complete two laps of the 170 m course (lower is better)
2025.human_reference: Specialist workforce: professional and commercial drone/UAV operators and FPV pilots. These are the people who would perform fine, rapid manual control of a drone in work settings.

2026.model_or_system: TII Racing autonomous drone (Technology Innovation Institute)
2026.metric: seconds (fastest autonomous lap time, lower is better)
2026.human_reference: Specialist workforce: people who fly drones or FPV aircraft in work settings (commercial and professional drone operators, including professional racing pilots), with the median operator as the reference point.
